title: Cache Miss
briefing: A messaging app shows the sender's profile card next to every message. Traffic builds to 20,000 requests per second over the first minute; 96% of requests read a profile, the rest update one.
Unlike news, nothing here is popular. There are 100 million profiles, and each read is equally likely to be any of them.

Profiles may be slightly out of date: a read can miss a change for up to 1 second. Read replicas are copies of the database that serve reads. They replay the primary's writes a fraction of a second behind it, and fall further behind when they're busy.
debrief: A cache works when the same keys are read again before they expire. Here each profile is read about once every 87 minutes on average: 100 million profiles shared among 19,200 reads a second. A cached profile has almost always expired, or was never fetched, before anyone asks for it again. Even the biggest cache served about 1% of reads.
Read replicas add read capacity instead. Each replica is a full copy of the database, so any of them can answer any read. Three large replicas share 19,200 reads a second, 6,400 each.

Copies aren't free: every replica replays every write. Replaying a write costs half what running it did, so 800 writes a second take a tenth of a large replica. With its 6,400 reads, each replica is about 74% busy.

Replicas are always a little behind the primary. An idle replica lags 0.2 seconds, and a busy one lags 0.2 ÷ (1 − busy): at 74% busy, about 0.8 seconds, inside the 1 second allowed. With two replicas, each would need 106% of its capacity: they fall further behind every second, serve stale profiles, then time out.
Replicas suit data that can be slightly old. The next level is about data that can't.

solutions.name: Three large read replicas
solutions.explanation: Each replica serves 6,400 reads a second and replays 800 writes: about 74% busy and 0.8 seconds behind the primary. The medium primary only handles the writes.

antiSolutions.name: The biggest cache
antiSolutions.explanation: A 128 GB cache in front of a large database. Profiles are almost never read twice before they expire, so it hits about 1% and the database drowns.

antiSolutions.name: The biggest database
antiSolutions.explanation: An xlarge database does 20,000 reads a second, and the writes take a tenth of it: 19,200 reads and 800 writes need 106%.

antiSolutions.name: Two large read replicas
antiSolutions.explanation: 9,600 reads each, plus replaying the writes: 106% busy. They fall behind and serve stale profiles, then time out.
